Each training example is a miniature regression problem. A hidden vector specifies a linear rule; the model sees several noisy input–output pairs from that rule and must predict the output at one new input. The rule changes from example to example. A small transformer learns from many such problems how to use the observations inside each prompt.

This page first defines the continuous problem, then explains what changes when numbers become tokens. The working configuration is **10 million frozen training examples, two input dimensions, 64 observations per prompt, noise standard deviation 0.001, and a roughly one-million-parameter model**. The interactive figures are illustrative draws from the stated process, not measurements from a trained model or records extracted from the training pool.

## The continuous problem {#sec-setup}

Let $d$ be the input dimension, $n$ the number of context observations, and $\sigma$ the noise standard deviation. To generate **one** example:

1. Draw a hidden coefficient vector $w\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d/d)$.
2. Independently draw $x_1,\ldots,x_n,x_*\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$.
3. Draw independent noises $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n,\epsilon_*\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, independent of $w$ and all inputs.
4. Form the observations and query target:

$$
y_i=w^\top x_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad
s_*=w^\top x_*,\qquad y_*=s_*+\epsilon_*.
$$ {#eq-generation}

The context is $D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$; the query input is $x_*$. The model receives their **quantized** representations and learns a distribution over the quantized noisy answer $y_*$. We also evaluate against the clean signal $s_*$. Neither $w$, the noise values, nor the unrounded numbers are exposed to the model. Noise affects outputs, not the underlying input coordinates. [Data generator](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/data.py).

There are two different sample counts: $n=64$ observations help infer the rule **within one prompt**, whereas $M=10{,}000{,}000$ training examples teach the transformer across **many independently drawn rules**. Increasing $M$ does not give a held-out prompt more observations. The context and query share $w$ within a prompt, so their outputs are not independent after marginalizing over that shared vector.

### Which quantities are Gaussian, and which have variance one?

For a fresh input $x$, the clean signal $s=w^\top x$ satisfies

$$
\mathbb E[s]=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(s)=\mathbb E_w\|w\|^2
=\operatorname{tr}(I_d/d)=1.
$$ {#eq-signal-variance}

This normalization keeps the **population signal variance** fixed as $d$ changes. Consequently

$$
\operatorname{Var}(y)=1+\sigma^2,\qquad
\mathrm{SNR}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(s)}{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}.
$$ {#eq-snr}

Here SNR is a variance ratio; the standard-deviation ratio is $1/\sigma$, and the decibel value is $-20\log_{10}\sigma$. At $\sigma=0.001$, these are $10^6$, $10^3$, and $60$ dB respectively.

The conditioning matters for the distribution:

| What is held fixed? | Distribution of the clean signal |
| --- | --- |
| One task's $w$; vary its input $x$ | $s\mid w\sim\mathcal N(0,\|w\|^2)$ |
| One input $x$; draw a new rule $w$ | $s\mid x\sim\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2/d)$ |
| Neither; draw both across the task population | A zero-centered Gaussian **variance mixture**, generally not Gaussian |

Adding output noise adds $\sigma^2$ to either conditional Gaussian variance. The variance-one statement is a population average: individual tasks have signal variance $\|w\|^2$, and their conditional SNR is $\|w\|^2/\sigma^2$.

For the present **$d=2$** Gaussian prior, the unconditional **clean** signal is exactly Laplace:

$$
s\sim\operatorname{Laplace}\!\left(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\right),\qquad
p(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\exp(-\sqrt 2|s|).
$$ {#eq-laplace}

One way to see this is to write $w_j=g_j/\sqrt d$ for independent standard normal $g_j$. Each product $g_jx_j/\sqrt d$ has characteristic function $(1+t^2/d)^{-1/2}$, so the sum has $(1+t^2/d)^{-d/2}$. For $d=2$ this is $(1+t^2/2)^{-1}$, the characteristic function of the Laplace law above. As $d$ grows, it tends to $e^{-t^2/2}$, the standard Gaussian characteristic function. The noisy marginal is the convolution of this clean law with $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$.

::: {.callout-note}
The variance $1$ belongs to the clean signal; it is **not** irreducible prediction error. Even if $w$ and $x_*$ were known exactly, the fresh noisy target would retain variance $\sigma^2$. Calling both quantities “intrinsic variance” would obscure the distinction. An exactly standard-Gaussian clean marginal would follow from a fixed unit-norm $w$ (or a prior supported on the unit sphere), which would change the implemented prior.
:::

::: {#fig-population}

### What must the context resolve?

In two dimensions, $w=(w_1,w_2)$ is the slope of the plane $s=w_1x_1+w_2x_2$. Points with the same clean output lie on parallel lines in the input plane, perpendicular to $w$. Seeing examples in different input directions helps determine both slopes. Repeated observations along nearly the same direction leave the perpendicular component uncertain.

With **continuous** observations, this has an exact Bayesian solution. If $X$ contains the $n$ context inputs as rows and $y$ their outputs, then

$$
\Sigma=(dI_d+X^\top X/\sigma^2)^{-1},\qquad
\mu=\Sigma X^\top y/\sigma^2,
$$
$$
s_*\mid D,x_*\sim\mathcal N(x_*^\top\mu,\;x_*^\top\Sigma x_*),\qquad
y_*\mid D,x_*\sim\mathcal N(x_*^\top\mu,\;x_*^\top\Sigma x_*+\sigma^2).
$$ {#eq-posterior}

The first variance describes uncertainty about the hidden rule; the extra $\sigma^2$ is fresh query noise. When $X^\top X\approx nI_d$, the average clean predictive variance is approximately $d\sigma^2/(n+d\sigma^2)$. This is an intuition for a well-covered design, not an exact finite-sample identity. Increasing $d$ at fixed $n$ makes inference harder even though signal variance stays one. For $n<d$, noiseless observations cannot determine all directions of $w$.

The implementation uses this continuous-data posterior as an optimistic reference. Applying the same formula to decoded token centers gives a **plug-in ridge approximation**, not the exact Bayesian answer to the quantized-input problem: rounding and clipping change the observation model. [Reference implementations](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/references.py).

## Turning numbers into tokens {#sec-quantization}

### The scalar codec

The current codec has $K=256$ equally spaced **centers**, including both endpoints of $[-A,A]=[-3,3]$:

$$
\Delta=\frac{2A}{K-1}=\frac{6}{255}\approx0.0235294,\qquad
c_k=-A+k\Delta,\quad k=0,\ldots,255.
$$

A scalar $z$ maps to its nearest center; midpoint ties go to the larger index and tails saturate at an endpoint. Equivalently, in exact arithmetic,

$$
q(z)=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,255]}
\left(\left\lfloor\frac{z+A}{\Delta}+\frac12\right\rfloor\right),\qquad
q=16a+b.
$$ {#eq-codec}

The index is stored as two base-16 **digit tokens** $a,b\in\{0,\ldots,15\}$. Their visible names are `0`–`9`, `A`–`F`; they are vocabulary entries, not characters passed through a text tokenizer. Every coordinate and every output uses the same codec. The implementation searches stored midpoints to handle floating-point ties consistently and rejects nonfinite values. [Scalar codec](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/codec.py).

Two base-16 digits provide 256 possible outputs with a small digit vocabulary and a short autoregressive answer; the complete answer distribution is still small enough to enumerate. At a fixed range, more levels would preserve more precision, while a single token per level would require a larger vocabulary. The chosen range and resolution are experimental design choices, not a claim of optimal quantization.

For example, $1\mapsto170\mapsto\texttt{A A}$ and decodes to $1$ exactly. Zero lies **between** centers 127 and 128, so $0\mapsto\texttt{8 0}$ and decodes to $3/255\approx0.011765$. There is no exact zero center. In the unclipped interior, the maximum rounding error is $\Delta/2\approx0.011765$.

### Quantization regimes and why they matter

The useful comparison is among **noise scale $\sigma$**, **grid spacing $\Delta$**, and **range $A$**. The labels below describe a continuous crossover, not sharp phase transitions.

| Regime | Scale relation | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Noise resolved by the grid | $\Delta\ll\sigma$ | Many output bins lie inside one noise standard deviation. Bin probabilities resolve the continuous noise distribution. |
| Noise and grid comparable | $\Delta\approx\sigma$ | Several neighboring answers can be plausible; bin boundaries materially affect the label distribution. |
| Noise mostly hidden by the grid | $\sigma\ll\Delta$ | Away from boundaries, changing the noise often leaves both answer tokens unchanged. Near a midpoint, even tiny noise can change the bin. |
| Saturation in the tails | $|z|>A$ | The codec loses tail magnitude. This can coexist with any of the three noise regimes. |

The justification comes from bin probabilities. For a known clean output $s$, define interior boundaries $b_k=(c_{k-1}+c_k)/2$ for $k=1,\ldots,K-1$, with $b_0=-\infty$ and $b_K=+\infty$. Then

$$
\Pr(q(s+\epsilon)=k\mid s)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b_{k+1}-s}{\sigma}\right)
-\Phi\!\left(\frac{b_k-s}{\sigma}\right).
$$ {#eq-bin-probability}

At an interior bin center, the probability of staying in that bin is $2\Phi(\Delta/(2\sigma))-1$. At a midpoint, the two adjacent bins each receive nearly half the mass when $\sigma\ll\Delta$. Thus “small noise” does not mean “deterministic tokens” uniformly over all clean signals.

At the default $\sigma=0.001$, $\Delta/\sigma\approx23.53$. The familiar uniform-rounding approximation gives $\Delta/\sqrt{12}\approx0.006792$ and variance $\Delta^2/12\approx4.61\times10^{-5}$, about 46 times the injected noise variance $10^{-6}$. This approximation assumes a smooth distribution across bins and negligible clipping; it is a scale comparison, **not** an independent-noise model guaranteed by the codec and **not** a universal MSE floor for the learned predictor.

Input quantization matters too. Writing $\tilde x=x+\delta_x$ and $\tilde y=y+\delta_y$ gives

$$
\tilde y=w^\top\tilde x+\epsilon+\delta_y-w^\top\delta_x.
$$

Under the same rough independent-rounding approximation, the extra context residual variance conditional on $w$ is $(1+\|w\|^2)\Delta^2/12$. Query-input rounding adds another source of uncertainty when evaluating against a continuous target. The exact token-conditioned problem must account for the input and output intervals jointly.

The finite range is a second tradeoff. A wider range clips less, but makes $\Delta$ larger if $K$ stays fixed. At $A=3$, a standard-Gaussian input coordinate lies outside the range with probability about **0.270%**. For the $d=2$ **clean** signal, @eq-laplace gives

$$
\Pr(|s|>3)=e^{-3\sqrt2}\approx1.437\%.
$$

Using a standard-Gaussian tail calculation for these outputs would understate clipping. Noisy-output clipping is a different probability, though close at $\sigma=0.001$. Also, landing in an endpoint **bin** does not necessarily mean the raw number was outside $[-3,3]$: the endpoint bin begins half a step inside the range. Actual saved-pool clipping fractions are recorded in dataset metadata.

::: {#fig-quantization}

## The working configuration {#sec-defaults}

The requested configuration is summarized below. It uses the newer delimited prompt; @sec-prompts compares it with the legacy format.

::: {#tbl-configuration}

| Component | Working setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frozen training pool | $M=10{,}000{,}000$ examples | Independently generated regression problems, saved once |
| Held-out evaluation pool | 1,024 examples | Separate draws; no additional test split in these launchers |
| Input dimension / context | $d=2$, $n=64$ | Two slopes to infer from 64 noisy observations |
| Prior / input law | $w\sim\mathcal N(0,I_2/2)$; $x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_2)$ | Population clean-signal variance $1$ |
| Output noise | $\sigma=0.001$ | Independent context and query draws; variance $10^{-6}$ |
| Scalar representation | 256 centers on $[-3,3]$; two base-16 digits | Shared across inputs and outputs |
| Model | Scratch Qwen2; **988,288 parameters** | Approximately 1M; 24-token delimited vocabulary |
| Architecture | 4 layers, hidden width 128, MLP width 512 | 4 query heads / 2 KV heads; tied input/output embeddings |
| Sequence capacity | 1,024 tokens | New format: 649 prompt tokens, 652 including answer and EOS |
| Training budget | 80,000 optimizer updates | Batch 128, microbatch 128 |
| Learning rate | $10^{-4}$ | Linear warmup over the first 2% of updates, then constant |
| Warmup start | $10^{-5}$ | One-tenth of the target rate; 1,600 warmup updates |
| Optimizer | AdamW; betas $(0.9,0.95)$, epsilon $10^{-8}$ | Weight decay 0.01; no gradient clipping |
| Precision | BF16 forward; FP32 master weights and optimizer | Loss computed in FP32 |

The 10M configuration discussed on this page. Data, architecture, and budget follow the delimited-format revision; the warmup starting rate is the requested working convention.
:::

There are $80{,}000\times128=10{,}240{,}000$ training **presentations**, equivalent to **1.024 passes** through the 10M pool: one full pass, then 240,000 examples from a new shuffle. Reshuffling does not redraw $w$, inputs, noises, or targets. The experiment does not set fixed generation or training seeds; saving a pool freezes its actual draws, and checkpoints retain RNG state for resumption.

To make “warmup from one-tenth” precise on this page, number updates from $s=1$ and let $W=1{,}600$. The intended schedule is

$$
\eta_s=
\begin{cases}
10^{-5}+(10^{-4}-10^{-5})\dfrac{s-1}{W-1}, & 1\leq s\leq W,\\[6pt]
10^{-4}, & W<s\leq80{,}000.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-warmup}

“Constant after warmup” refers to the learning rate; AdamW's weight decay remains active. The model uses causal attention, RoPE, RMSNorm and gated SiLU, with no attention dropout or sliding window. Parameters are initialized from scratch; it does not start from pretrained language-model weights.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Configuration provenance and launcher differences"}
The [delimited-format revision `c576954`](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/tree/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression) supplies the 10M pool, 24-token codec and 988,288-parameter model. Its checked-in launcher warms from zero. The later [legacy comparison revision `22fbb14`](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/tree/22fbb14dd3cb9bd5fcaf469cf01ba885728a1397/noisy-regression), checked out when this writeup was prepared, uses a 1M pool, the legacy 20-token codec and warmup from zero. Therefore the 10M / $10^{-5}$ warmup-start combination above is the **requested working specification**, not a claim that either unmodified launcher reproduces it.

In the inspected constant-LR scheduler, setting the minimum rate to $10^{-5}$ gives $10^{-5}+9\times10^{-5}s/W$ during warmup: its first applied rate is $1.005625\times10^{-5}$ rather than exactly $10^{-5}$. @eq-warmup states the desired endpoint convention explicitly. This page changes documentation, not experiment code or saved run manifests. [Scheduler implementation](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/model.py).
:::

### Explore a two-dimensional task

In @fig-geometry, the left panel keeps both input coordinates visible. The colored background is the hidden clean rule, circles are noisy observations, and the star is the query. The right panel shows the posterior over the **two coefficients**, so you can see how the context identifies the plane. At low noise its uncertainty region becomes very small; its axes automatically zoom.

Try increasing noise to $0.1$, reducing the context to one or two observations, rotating the hidden rule, and showing quantized inputs. Changing $n$ reuses a prefix of the same observations; changing noise rescales the same noise draws. This makes the effect of each control easier to compare. Drawing a new task samples a fresh $w$ from the stated prior; manually changing its angle or norm explores a chosen rule conditional on that $w$.

## What the model actually sees {#sec-prompts}

There is no English instruction in the actual training input. The displayed spaces and line breaks below make tokens readable; they are not extra tokens. Each digit and each bracketed marker is one vocabulary entry. The hidden coefficient vector is shared by all observations in a prompt and omitted from the sequence.

### A concrete miniature example

For readability, first use just three observations, with the illustrative hidden rule $w=(0.6,-0.8)$:

| Role | Continuous input $x$ | Clean output $s$ | Noise $\epsilon$ | Observed output $y$ | Encoded $x$; encoded $y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Context 1 | $(1,0)$ | $0.6$ | $0.001$ | $0.601$ | `A A 8 0`; `9 9` |
| Context 2 | $(0,1)$ | $-0.8$ | $-0.001$ | $-0.801$ | `8 0 A A`; `5 D` |
| Context 3 | $(-1,1)$ | $-1.4$ | $0.0005$ | $-1.3995$ | `5 5 A A`; `4 4` |
| Query | $(0.5,-0.5)$ | $0.7$ | $0.001$ | $0.701$ | `9 5 6 A`; `9 D` |

The answer `9 D` is index $16\times9+13=157$, which decodes to $0.694117647\ldots$, not the unrounded target $0.701$. The table's latent values explain how the example was made; they are not included in either prompt.

#### Legacy: shared observation and query markers

**Prompt supplied to the model:**

```text
[BOS]
[X] A A 8 0 [Y] 9 9
[X] 8 0 A A [Y] 5 D
[X] 5 5 A A [Y] 4 4
[X] 9 5 6 A [Y]
```

**Supervised continuation:**

```text
9 D
```

Adjacent coordinate digit pairs are separated by their fixed positions, with no explicit coordinate separator. Every observation is eight tokens at $d=2$. The final `[X] ... [Y]` is the query; there is no distinct query marker, observation terminator or EOS. The vocabulary is 16 digits plus `[X]`, `[Y]`, `[PAD]`, `[BOS]`, totaling **20 tokens**. The four-layer model has **987,776 parameters**. [Legacy codec](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/22fbb14dd3cb9bd5fcaf469cf01ba885728a1397/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/codec.py).

#### New: explicit coordinate and observation boundaries

**The same numerical example as a new-format prompt:**

```text
[BOS]
[X] A A [SEP] 8 0 [Y] 9 9 [EOO]
[X] 8 0 [SEP] A A [Y] 5 D [EOO]
[X] 5 5 [SEP] A A [Y] 4 4 [EOO]
[QUERY] [X] 9 5 [SEP] 6 A [Y]
```

**Supervised continuation:**

```text
9 D [EOS]
```

`[SEP]` separates coordinates within $x$; `[EOO]` ends a complete observed $(x,y)$ pair. `[QUERY]` announces the held-out input, and `[EOS]` terminates its answer. Each observation now takes ten tokens. The vocabulary is 16 digits plus `[X]`, `[SEP]`, `[Y]`, `[EOO]`, `[QUERY]`, `[PAD]`, `[BOS]`, `[EOS]`, totaling **24 tokens**. These extra four embeddings account for the parameter increase of $4\times128=512$. [Delimited codec](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/codec.py).

Explicit boundaries make the structure available through dedicated tokens instead of only fixed positions. That is an architectural motivation, **not evidence that the new format learns better**. It also lengthens the sequence and adds a termination loss, so a comparison should account for both effects. The 1M legacy pool and 10M new pool are an additional confound if comparing those particular runs.

### Lengths and the training objective

| At $d=2$, $n=64$ | Legacy | New |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context block | $64\times8=512$ | $64\times10=640$ |
| BOS plus query prefix | $1+6=7$ | $1+8=9$ |
| Prompt, through the query `[Y]` | **519** tokens | **649** tokens |
| Supervised continuation | 2 answer digits | 2 answer digits + `[EOS]` |
| Complete training sequence | **521** tokens | **652** tokens |

Teacher forcing supplies the complete sequence during training, but the causal mask prevents seeing future tokens. Context values serve as conditioning information and receive no loss. If the two answer digits are $a,b$, the answer loss is

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{answer}}
=-\log p_\theta(a\mid\text{prompt})
-\log p_\theta(b\mid\text{prompt},a).
$$

Both answer softmaxes are restricted to the 16 digit IDs. The new format additionally trains $-\log p_\theta(\texttt{[EOS]}\mid\text{prompt},a,b)$ using the full 24-token vocabulary. The optimization loss sums the applicable token terms, then averages over examples. Reported **answer NLL** remains the two-digit quantity for comparability. No loss is applied to `[SEP]`, `[EOO]` or the other prompt markers. [Loss implementation](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/noisy_regression/model.py).

## Reading the evaluation {#sec-evaluation}

There are only 256 possible numeric answers. The evaluator enumerates their exact autoregressive probabilities, $p(k)=p(a)p(b\mid a)$, instead of estimating them by sampling completions. Their decoded mean is $\hat y=\sum_kp(k)c_k$; unlike an individual decoded answer, this mean can lie between grid centers.

**MSE** compares that mean with the continuous clean target $s_*$ or noisy target $y_*$. **NLL** scores the corresponding quantized target bin. **Exact pass@$k$** is $1-(1-p(q(\mathrm{target})))^k$, the success probability of $k$ independent samples when success means matching that bin. The EOS loss is separate from this 256-value answer distribution. These metrics answer different questions: predicting a continuous mean accurately and assigning high probability to one discrete bin need not rank predictors identically. [Evaluation definitions](https://github.com/VincentWangzt/maxrl/blob/c576954f9c9cd9ced1b6522bcea33057f529ae68/noisy-regression/METRICS.md).

At this very small $\sigma$, the continuous task has high SNR, while the model still faces uncertainty from quantized coordinates, finite context and clipping. The continuous Bayesian reference has access to more precise information than the transformer. A gap to that reference therefore includes information lost at tokenization, as well as any error in learning to use the context.
